rows.label: Share of people in conflict-affected populations with a mental disorder

source.title: Charlson et al. (2019), New WHO prevalence estimates of mental disorders in conflict settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis, The Lancet 394:240-248, doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(19)30934-1
source.quote: The mean prevalence of mental disorders (depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia) was 22.1% (95% UI 18.8-25.7) at any point in time in the conflict-affected populations assessed.

rows.explainer: The WHO's point prevalence of depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia in populations that lived through conflict in the previous ten years, with its uncertainty interval as the range. Read by every model of ours that counts the mental-health gain of relief, protection or education for people displaced by or living through conflict.

rows.label: Protection: improvement in mental health for participants with a disorder (SD)

source.title: Purgato et al. (2018), Psychological therapies for the treatment of mental disorders in low- and middle-income countries affected by humanitarian crises, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD011849.pub2
source.note: Focused psychological and psychosocial interventions in humanitarian settings reduce post-traumatic stress, depression and anxiety symptoms by small to moderate amounts. A broad protection programme (community-based protection, monitoring and referral, mediation, case management and detention visits for fewer) delivers much less of that care per participant: 0.2 SD, from 0.05 to 0.4.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.2 SD (0.05-0.4), for broad protection work: the reference class is focused psychosocial support in humanitarian settings, which finds small to moderate falls in symptoms (Purgato et al. 2018); community protection, monitoring, referral and case management for a few do less per participant, so below it.

rows.label: Length of an episode of acute illness

source.title: Lamberti, Fischer Walker and Black (2012), Systematic review of diarrhea duration and severity in children and adults in low- and middle-income countries, BMC Public Health 12:276, doi:10.1186/1471-2458-12-276
source.quote: On average, mild episodes last 4.3 days, and severe episodes last 8.4 days and cause dehydration in 84.6% of cases.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, five days (three to eleven; 0.014 years): the reference class is the measured length of the acute illnesses relief averts. A systematic review of diarrhoea in low- and middle-income countries finds mild episodes last 4.3 days and severe ones 8.4 (Lamberti et al. 2012); malaria and respiratory episodes treated or self-limiting last about as long. Most episodes averted are mild, so five days, with severe and untreated episodes at the top. Read by every relief model of ours that counts acute illness averted.

rows.label: Shelter: years the shelter or repair is used

source.title: IFRC, Transitional shelters: eight designs (2012), design sheets B3 (Pakistan 2010) and B7 (Indonesia, Aceh 2005)
source.note: Pakistan's 2010 timber-frame and plastic-sheeting shelter (https://mail.shelterprojects.org/tshelter-8designs/8designs2012/B3-Pakistan-2010.pdf): 'Anticipated lifespan: 24 months'; Haiti's 2010 steel-frame shelter the same; Aceh's galvanised steel frame at least five years.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 2 years (1-5), for a crisis shelter programme's mix: tents, tarpaulins and kits are used up within about a year; the IFRC's transitional shelter designs are built to last from 24 months (timber or steel frames with plastic sheeting, Pakistan and Haiti 2010) to at least five years (steel frames, Aceh 2005); repaired and rebuilt homes last longer, but displaced families move on.

rows.label: Shelter: episodes of acute illness averted per person reached

source.title: Connolly et al. (2004), Communicable diseases in complex emergencies: impact and challenges, The Lancet 364:1974-1983, doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(04)17481-3
source.quote: Factors promoting disease transmission interact synergistically leading to high incidence rates of diarrhoea, respiratory infection, malaria, and measles.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.03 episodes (0-0.1): crowding and exposure drive the high rates of respiratory infection and diarrhoea in emergencies (Connolly et al. 2004), and shelter, blankets, drainage and site work act on a part of that; no trial measures it, so the range runs from nothing to a tenth of an episode.

rows.label: WASH: diarrhoeal deaths per person-year in the crisis sites
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.0008 (0.0004-0.002): the Global Burden of Disease puts diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa at about 50 per 100,000 a year (0.0005); camps and crowded sites with broken water systems (Sudan, Yemen, Somalia, Gaza, the DRC) run higher, with cholera outbreaks, while Ukraine's and Lebanon's run far lower. Read by the emergency WASH branches of our refugee-relief models.

rows.label: WASH: fall in diarrhoeal deaths among the people served

source.title: Wolf et al. (2022), Effectiveness of interventions to improve drinking water, sanitation, and handwashing with soap on risk of diarrhoeal disease in children in low-income and middle-income settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis, The Lancet 400:48-59
source.note: Water treatment, sanitation and hygiene each cut diarrhoea by roughly a fifth to a third where used; Yates et al. (2017) find the evidence on emergency WASH thin. 15%, 3-35%.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 15% (3-35%): meta-analyses find water treatment, sanitation and hygiene each cut diarrhoea by roughly a fifth to a third where they are used (Wolf et al. 2022), but emergency WASH reaches many people with light services (water trucking, hygiene sessions) and its own evidence is thin (Yates et al. 2017 systematic review).

rows.label: WASH: diarrhoea episodes averted per person-year of service
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.1 episodes (0.02-0.3): people in crises have about one to three episodes of diarrhoea a year, children more; the 15% fall (wash_crisis_diarrhoea_death_reduction) applied to about 0.7 episodes.

rows.label: Legal assistance: share of participants counselled or assisted on a legal problem
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 30% (15-50%): many participants of displacement legal aid get legal information in group sessions or online; the rest individual counselling, legal assistance or representation. Read by the information, counselling and legal assistance branches of our refugee-relief models.

rows.label: Legal assistance: consumption gain for a resolved case
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 5% (1-15%): identity documents and legal stay open formal work, aid registration, schooling and health care and end the risk of detention; secure housing and land avert eviction. No study measures the income effect of legal aid for displaced people; anchored on cash-equivalent valuations of documentation in livelihoods studies being small but lasting.

rows.label: Legal assistance: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 3 years (1-6): a document or legal status lasts, but displaced people move on and circumstances change.

rows.label: People in need of humanitarian aid worldwide, 2025

source.title: Norwegian Refugee Council, Annual Report from the Board 2025 (published 18 June 2026)
source.quote: prioritising 114 million people out of the 305.1 million people in need

rows.explainer: OCHA's global figure for 2025, as NRC's board report gives it: the people the year's humanitarian funding serves.

rows.label: Humanitarian appeals funding received, 2025 (US$)

source.title: ALNAP, The State of the Humanitarian System 2026, 1.1 The reality of funding gaps
source.quote: Only 35% of the total 2025 appeals target was met.

rows.explainer: Funding received against the 2025 UN-coordinated appeals, 'to US$16.6 billion', against a shortfall of US$30.5 billion (same page, from OCHA's Financial Tracking Service); refugee response plans are part of it. Aid given outside the appeals (the Red Cross movement, MSF, bilateral aid) is left out, so aid per person is understated.

rows.label: Funding: share of a year's humanitarian funding kept or added by NGOs' collective funding advocacy

source.title: OECD, International aid fell sharply in 2025 (preliminary 2025 data, press release, 9 April 2026)
source.note: Donors' humanitarian aid fell 35.8% in 2025. 1% of 2025's funding is keeping about 2% of the cut (0.4-7% across the range).

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 1% (0.2-4%), for the humanitarian NGOs' collective advocacy on the funding gap: donors' humanitarian aid fell 35.8% in 2025 (OECD, preliminary 2025 data), a cut of about 56% of what was left; advocacy may have kept some budgets from falling further and steered some to underfunded crises and sectors. 1% of 2025's funding is keeping about 2% of the cut: the cuts were driven by budget decisions that advocacy barely moved, chiefly the US's. Each organisation's share of the collective effort is its own model's.

rows.label: Funding: share of the money kept or added that comes from other aid
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 60% (30-90%): humanitarian budgets kept are partly taken from development aid within the same aid totals; the rest from donors' general spending. Read by every model of ours valuing humanitarian funding advocacy.
